title: Building Agents (the hard parts!) - Rita Kozlov, Cloudflare

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

summary:
Rita Kozlov introduces Cloudflare's developer platform and mission, noting that 20% of internet traffic flows through Cloudflare. She highlights rapid AI adoption: over 75% of knowledge workers now use AI for augmentation, surpassing Gartner's 2030 predictions, and over 76% of developers use AI in their development process. She traces the evolution of AI workloads from training to inference (citing OpenAI's o1 and DeepSeek) and identifies full automation via agents as the next phase, noting businesses already see 20% revenue increases in sales automation, 90% faster support response times, and 50-75% time savings.

Kozlov breaks agents into four components: (1) the client/interface for human interaction, (2) AI reasoning/thinking, (3) workflows for executing actions, and (4) tools for taking actions. She walks through a CRM agent example requiring WebRTC, speech-to-text, chat UI hosting, a gateway for caching/evals, an LLM, a workflow agent to track actions, tool connections, and human-in-the-loop verification.

She focuses on tools, highlighting Anthropic's MCP standard introduced in November. The real breakthrough is that LLMs became excellent at tool calling, and MCP provides a client-server architecture for exposing APIs to LLMs via resources, prompts, tooling, and sampling. MCP's tricky parts include transport protocols (OAuth over SSE/WebSockets) and memory. Cloudflare's Agents SDK addresses these with built-in OAuth transport, state management via Durable Objects, real-time WebSocket communication, and React integration. She demonstrates a book recommendation MCP server with persistent genre preferences, emphasizing that built-in state eliminates separate database setup and scales automatically. Companies like Atlassian, Asana, Stripe, and Intercom are building MCP servers this way.

For workflows, Kozlov presents a Knock notification management example: a credit card approval agent requiring human-in-the-loop. The implementation uses the Agents SDK React library for chat, wraps card issuance in a require-human-input tool, defers tool execution pending approval via Knock notifications, routes approval webhooks back to the correct Durable Object by user ID, resumes the paused tool call upon approval, and uses state management to prevent duplicate actions.

For the client component, she notes MCP servers can be accessed through existing tools like Cursor, Claude, and ChatGPT, or through custom apps and voice interfaces using Cloudflare's WebRTC-to-WebSocket translation. She defers model selection discussion to other conference talks.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Cloudflare Mission
sections.summary: Rita Kozlov introduces herself as VP of Product for Cloudflare's developer platform. She explains Cloudflare's mission for developers: making it easy to bring ideas from first line of code to production at scale.

sections.title: AI Adoption Statistics and Shift to Automation
sections.summary: Kozlov presents AI adoption statistics showing rapid growth, with 75%+ knowledge workers and 76%+ developers using AI. She traces workload evolution from training to inference (citing OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek) and identifies full automation via agents as the next phase, with businesses already seeing significant productivity gains.

sections.title: Four Components of Agent Architecture
sections.summary: Agents consist of four components: client/interface, AI reasoning/thinking, workflows for execution, and tools for taking actions. A CRM agent example illustrates the need for WebRTC, speech-to-text, chat UI, gateway, LLM, workflow agent, tool connections, and human-in-the-loop verification.

sections.title: MCP Standard and Core Concepts
sections.summary: Kozlov discusses Anthropic's MCP standard, noting the real breakthrough is LLMs becoming good at tool calling. MCP core concepts include resources, prompts, tooling, and sampling. She observes sampling appears unused in production. Tricky parts include transport protocol (OAuth over SSE/WebSockets) and memory.

sections.title: Cloudflare Agents SDK and MCP Server Demo
sections.summary: Kozlov introduces Cloudflare's Agents SDK for handling MCP's hard parts: OAuth transport, state management via Durable Objects, WebSocket communication, and React integration. She demonstrates deploying a book recommendation MCP server with persistent genre preferences using tools and personalized prompts.

sections.title: MCP Server Benefits and Adoption
sections.summary: Kozlov explains that built-in state in MCP agents eliminates the need for separate databases, connection management, and scaling concerns. State persists regardless of the client used. Companies like Atlassian, Asana, Stripe, and Intercom are building MCP servers on Cloudflare this way. A deploy button enables setup in under a minute.

sections.title: Workflows and Human-in-the-Loop: Knock Example
sections.summary: Kozlov covers the workflow coordination component, explaining human-in-the-loop workflows require long-running tasks that can resume after minutes to months. She walks through a Knock notification management example: a credit card approval agent using the Agents SDK React library, require_human_input tool wrapping, deferred tool execution pending Knock approval notifications, webhook routing back to the correct Durable Object by user ID, resuming paused tool calls upon approval, and state-based duplicate action prevention.

sections.title: Client Component and Conclusion
sections.summary: Kozlov briefly defers model/reasoning selection to other conference talks. She explains the client component: MCP servers can be accessed through existing tools like Cursor, Claude, and ChatGPT, or through custom apps and voice interfaces using Cloudflare's WebRTC-to-WebSocket translation. She concludes by reiterating the four agent components and recommending the Agents SDK for quick startup.

demonstrations: Deploying an MCP server on Cloudflare using the Agents SDK with a book recommendation example, showing how to define an MCP class extending MCP_agent, set initial empty state, add an 'add genre' tool to persist preferences, and a 'get recommendations' tool with personalized prompts based on previously saved genres

Building a human-in-the-loop credit card approval agent with Knock using the Agents SDK: creating a chat interface via use_agent from the agents React library, wrapping card issuance in require_human_input tool, deferring tool execution until approval via Knock notifications, routing webhooks back to the correct Durable Object by user ID, resuming the paused tool call upon approval, and using state to prevent duplicate provisioning
limitations: MCP transport protocol over SSE and WebSockets with OAuth is tricky to implement manually
Memory/state management for MCP servers is challenging without built-in solutions
MCP sampling appears unused in production despite being a core concept
Human-in-the-loop workflows require handling long-running tasks that can take minutes to months, with complexities around retries, horizontal scaling, and WebSocket persistence
Preventing duplicate actions in async agent workflows requires careful state management
quantitativeClaims: About 20% of internet traffic flows through Cloudflare
Over 75% of knowledge workers use AI to augment their work today, surpassing Gartner's 2030 prediction of 50%
Over 76% of developers use AI as part of their development process
Some businesses see 20% revenue increases from adopting agents in sales automation
Some businesses see 90% faster response times to support using AI agents
People see about 50-75% time savings when using agents
Deploying an initial MCP server on Cloudflare takes less than a minute via a deploy button
